The sample questionnaire included with the Committee's brief deals with Richmond and reveals that the actual response to the business relocation question was: "impossible to say for certain, but this percentage is likely to be very low." This type of observation, while arguably somewhat probative, does not establish that there has been no significant business relocation in the past 10 years.
Turning our attention to the actual data contained in the Committee's brief, we have some doubts as to the completeness of the picture of economic interaction presented.

City to suburb population movement statistics are absent; however, much of the presented information concerns movements of workers, raw materials, and dollars from the base municipality to the suburbs. Variables A and B both relate to residents of base municipalities who work in the areas that would be included in the expanded zones. Variable C reflects the use of base municipality raw materials in the expanded commercial zone. Variable D deals with the percentage of new area sales purchased with central city dollars. While in a few cases a substantial degree of dependence on the base municipality is indicated, the figures are generally low. Our difficulty with these statistics is
The low level of some of these indicators is quite compatible with our notions of the contemporary configuration of the urban environment. The post-war boom in suburban residential development would account for the modest percentage of central city residents commuting to work in the suburbs. Furthermore, the central city has never acted as a significant source of raw materials.
